#80671. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3058 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report.
  • Sources indicate that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

Sources indicate that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

Industry observers note that we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

It has been revealed that power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

It has been revealed that the second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

In a recent development, which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

It has been revealed that the formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

In a recent development, relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

Recent findings suggest that in each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

On 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

Recent findings suggest that before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

The measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

According to recent reports, it returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any upcoming starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Recent findings suggest that before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

This time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

It has been revealed that each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

It has been revealed that one detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

It has been revealed that good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a fresh colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

In a recent development, an agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and said it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

According to recent reports, the --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

An agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer new to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

Industry observers note that these are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this second piece we turn our focus from models to the architectural and hardware choices Chinese companies have made as openness becomes the norm.

For AI researchers and developers contributing to and relying on the open source ecosystem and for policymakers understanding the rapidly changing environment, architectural preferences, modality diversification, license permissiveness, small model popularity, and growing adoption of Chinese hardware point to leadership strategies across a multitude of paths. DeepSeek R1's own characteristics inspired overlap and competition, and contributed to heavier focus on domestic hardware in China.

In the past year, leading models from the Chinese community had almost unanimously moved toward Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, including Kimi K2, MiniMax M2, and Qwen3. R1 itself was an MoE model, it also proved a crucial point: strong reasoning could be open, reproducible, and engineered in practice. Under China's real-world constraints, maintaining high capability while controlling cost, and ensuring models could be trained, deployed, and widely adopted, MoE emerged as a natural solution.

MoE is like a controllable compute distribution system; under a single capability framework, compute resources are allocated across requests and deployment environments by dynamically activating different numbers of experts according to task complexity and value. More importantly, it does not require every inference to consume the full set of resources, nor does it assume that all deployment environments share identical hardware conditions.

The overall direction of Chinese open-source models in 2025 was clear: not necessarily the strongest possible performance, but ability to operate sustainably, deploy flexibly, and evolve continuously, achieving the best cost performance balance.

Industry observers note that starting in February 2025, open-source activity was no longer focused only on text models. It quickly expanded into multimodal and agent-based directions: Any-to-Any models, text-to-image, image-to-video, text-to-video, TTS, 3D, and agents all progressed in parallel. What the community pushed forward was not just model weights, but a full set of engineering assets, including inference deployment, datasets and evaluation, toolchains, workflows, and edge-to-cloud coordination. The parallel emergence of video generation tools, 3D components, distillation datasets, and agent frameworks pointed to something larger than isolated breakthroughs---it pointed to reusable system-level capabilities.

According to recent reports, the competition to lead similar to DeepSeek in a non-text modality heated up. StepFun's released high performance multimodal models, excelling in audio, video, and image generation and processing or editing. Their latest speech-to-speech model Step-Audio-R1.1 boasts state-of-the-art performance, beating proprietary models. Tencent also reflected this shift through open-source work in video and 3D. Its Hunyuan Video models and projects such as Hunyuan 3D reflect growing competition beyond text-centric models.

Models in the 0.5B--30B range were easier to run locally, fine-tune, and integrate into business systems and agent workflows. For example: Among the Qwen series, Qwen 1.5-0.5B has the most derivative models. In environments with limited compute or strict compliance requirements, these models were far better suited for long-term operation. At the same time, leading players often used large MoE models in the 100B--700B range as capability ceilings or "teacher models," then distilled those capabilities down into many smaller models. This created a clear structure: a few very large models at the top, and many practical models underneath. The growing share of small models in monthly summaries reflected real usage needs in the community.

https://huggingface.co/spaces/cfahlgren1/hub-model-tree-stats.

According to recent reports, after R1, Apache 2.0 became close to the default choice for open models from the Chinese community. More permissive licenses lowered the friction around using, modifying, and deploying models in production, making it much easier for companies to move open models into real systems. Familiarity with standard licenses, such as Apache 2.0 and MIT, similarly eased usage; prescriptive and tailored licenses add friction through unfamiliarity and newly introduced legal barriers, contributing to the decline seen in the graph below.

Based on the releases of all organizations shown in Chinese Open Source Heatmap.

In 2025, model releases increasingly aligned with inference frameworks, quantization formats, serving engines, and edge runtimes. A prominent goal was no longer just to make weights downloadable, but to ensure that models could run directly on target domestic hardware---and run reliably and efficiently. This change was most visible on the inference side. For example, With DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, both Huawei Ascend and Cambricon chips achieved day-zero support, not as cloud demos, but as reproducible inference pipelines released alongside the weights, enabling developers to validate real-world performance directly.

At the same time, training-side signals began to appear. Ant Group's Ling open models use optimized training on domestic AI chips to achieve near NVIDIA H800 performance, cutting the cost of training 1 trillion tokens by about 20%. Baidu's open Qianfan-VL models clearly documented that the model was trained on a cluster of more than 5,000 Baidu Kunlun P800 accelerators, their flagship AI chip, with details on parallelization and efficiency. At the beginning of 2026, Zhipu's GLM-Image and China Telecom's latest open model - TeleChat3, were both confirmed as being trained entirely on domestic chips. These disclosures highlighted that domestic computers were no longer limited to inference, but had started to enter key stages of the training pipeline.

On the serving and infrastructure side, engineering capabilities are being systematically open-sourced. Moonshot AI released its serving system: Mooncake, and explicitly supported features such as prefill/decoding separation. By open-sourcing production-grade experience, these efforts significantly raised the baseline for deployment and operations across the community, making it easier to run models reliably at scale. This direction was echoed across the ecosystem. Baidu's FastDeploy 2.0 emphasized extreme quantization and cluster-level optimization to reduce inference costs under tight compute budgets. Alibaba's Qwen ecosystem pursued full-stack integration, tightly aligning models, inference frameworks, quantization strategies, and cloud deployment workflows to minimize friction from development to production. Still, reports of compute constraints in China threaten expansion; Zhipu AI is reportedly restricting usage amid a computing crunch.

According to recent reports, when models, tools, and engineering are delivered together, the ecosystem no longer grows by adding projects, but by structurally differentiating on a shared foundation-and beginning to evolve on its own. How China will respond to U.S. hardware sales and export controls as NVIDIA sells H200s continues to be an open question. Read more about the shifting global compute landscape here.

In a recent development, the "DeepSeek Moment" of January 2025 did more than trigger a wave of new open models. It forced a deeper reconsideration of how AI systems should be built when open source is no longer optional but foundational and why those underlying choices now carry strategic weight.

In a recent development, chinese companies are no longer optimizing isolated models. Instead, they are pursuing distinct architectural paths aimed at building full ecosystems suited to an open-source world. In an increasingly commoditized model landscape, these decisions signal a clear shift in competition from model performance to system design.

Our next blog will go deeper into organizational wins and share some of what we expect to see in 2026.

When documenting our own system architectures and evaluating different approaches, I've found InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) incredibly valuable—it turns plain English system descriptions into architecture diagrams that you can iterate on through conversation. Makes it much easier to communicate architectural trade-offs and maintain living documentation.

One point that strikes me is that Chinese open source seems to have internalized something that the West still treats as secondary: when models become commodities, the real differentiator becomes systemic operability. It's not about "the best weight," but about who delivers a complete system—from training to inference—that works under real cost, hardware, and compliance constraints. This completely changes the axis of competition.

The open-world crime game has attracted enormous attention worldwide, with fans taking time off work to play it. According to French broadcaster TF1, requests for annual leave in France increased by 8% around the game’s launch. Now, the game has been introduced to the older generations.

On November 20, residents at the Domitys senior living facility in Serris, Seine-et-Marne, were introduced to GTA 6 as part of an organized gaming session.

As reported by ICI Paris Île-de-France, the residents swapped their usual activities for an opportunity to explore the game’s virtual world, with many particularly enjoying its boat-driving sequences.

82-year-old Jacqueline was among the most enthusiastic participants, successfully collecting two packages of cocaine during a mission. “I had never touched a controller before 9am this morning. And by 2:30pm, I was fishing out two packages of drugs,” she joked.

Another resident, 86-year-old Lucienne, was equally impressed by the game’s visuals, describing them as incredible and comparing the experience to watching a real film.

Meanwhile, 75-year-old Yvan admitted that the controls were difficult to master, joking that he was no longer 20 and struggled to keep up with the action.

Staff explained that the residents had found driving and shooting particularly challenging, but enjoyed exploring the environment by boat.

According to recent reports, the best thing about agent skills is upskilling your agents on hard problems. There are two ways to look at that:.

This blog post walks through the process of using a fresh tool, upskill, to generate and evaluate agent skills with large models and use them with smaller models. We will benchmark upskill on the task of writing CUDA kernels for diffusers models, but the process is generally useful for cutting costs, or using smaller models on hard and domain-specific problems.

In case you missed it, agent skills are taking the coding agent game by storm. In fact, they’re a straightforward concept to define model context as files, like instructions as markdown and code as scripts. The file format makes them easy to generate, share, and review. In short, they’re a practical medium to share capabilities across models and tools, and they're most useful in specific domains or hard problems. Not stuff the model can do well anyway.

This post showcases this process by using Claude to generate a Skill file that can be used by open source models for a complex and specialized task: write CUDA kernels. We first tried a simple skill based on existing documentation, and we found that it improved performance for some others, but not all. In fact, it could even degrade performance or increase token usage for some models. Check out the plot below to see the performance of the model with and without the basic skill.

Now, let's walk through how you can use upskill to upskill your agents on hard problems, and measure performance.

First, we use Claude Code to build a kernel interactively and export the trace. We worked through the process by instructing, validating, and adding documentation links. This somewhat naive process is vital to reveal the models' initial challenges. In fact, you can iterate on this multiple times, by trying to solve the task with draft versions of the skill, and experimenting with smaller models. Each time, you can instruct the agent to improve the skill and test it on the smaller model.

Here's an example of the skill that we created and have been using to build kernels. We started from this agent trace where the agent was able to build a kernel, but not without some help.

In a recent development, once the teacher model has performed the task, we need them to make a skill. There are a number of effective ways to do this.

According to recent reports, in most cases, the first 2 options result in functional skills. However, the performance of an agent with the skill is unknown. That’s where upskill is useful, because it will also generate test cases for your skill based on the trace. It then compares the results under both scenarios: using the trace, or applying the skill. We see below that the original model (Claude Opus) met the same performance with and without the skill. This means the skill captured the task for this model. Great!

Sources indicate that finally, we need to transfer our newly created skill to the tool or model we intend to use. Most tools like codex, cursor, and opencode have settled on a consistent format for skills, which is a directory at {agent}/skills/{skill_name}/SKILL.md , so we just need to copy the skill directory to this location.

Recent findings suggest that with upskill we can pass a skill and a set of models to the eval command and upskill will run the test cases on those models with and without the skill to compare performance. We can see here that the skill increases accuracy on some open models, but not on all.

Sources indicate that in this case, we might want to iterate further on the gpt-oss skills by regenerating the skill. We can do upskill generate --from {skill}.

Recent findings suggest that there is more to agent skills than model performance. Often agents can reach a given accuracy with or without a skill, they just need to consume more tokens to get there. For recurring tasks, we want to optimize agents to use less tokens to achieve the same accuracy. The results below reveal another dimension to the skill. Some models are significantly reducing their performance token usage, whilst others are using more tokens with the skill. For example, with moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Thinking the skill is clearly effective in terms of accuracy and token usage. However, for Claude Opus 4.5 there is no clear performance increase and an increase in token usage, so you would not want to use this skill with Claude Opus 4.5.

Industry observers note that tldr; try out and evaluate models with the skills you create. Use upskill eval or a similar tool to evaluate the models performance with and without skills.

That’s the high level end to end of upskilling your coding agents on hard problems. Try out upskill now like this:.

Industry observers note that we have a high level understanding of how we can upskill an agent. Let’s now look at the use case we solved for writing CUDA kernels.

According to recent reports, we didn’t just want to write kernel code, but understand the full kernel-builder workflow: project structure, build.toml configuration, architecture-specific optimizations, and PyTorch bindings. This tutorial reveals how upskill creates validated skills that actually work.

The kernel-builder-cuda-kernels skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about CUDA development: which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

And Claude will create the complete project structure, CUDA implementation, and build configuration—following the exact conventions that kernel-builder expects.

This isn't about generating boilerplate. The skill encodes domain expertise: H100 uses compute capability 9.0, shared memory should be aligned to 128 bytes, async memory copies require __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900. Knowledge that would take hours to gather from documentation gets packaged into ~500 tokens that load on demand.

Industry observers note that that's it. Upskill uses Anthropic Claude Opus-4.5 model by default but also supports OpenAI and local models via OpenAI-compatible endpoints as generators. We want to use the more expensive and higher quality models to generate skills, and the smaller ones to use them. Think robin hood.

Let's walk through generating a skill that teaches agents how to build CUDA kernels with HuggingFace's kernels library.

Also, we could start from an existing skill and add to it:.

upskill loads the existing skill, applies your improvements, and re-evaluates to ensure the changes help.

upskill creates a skill, generates test cases, evaluates performance, and refines based on failures:.

The baseline shows how the model performs without any skill. The "with skill" result shows performance after the skill is injected into context. A 35% improvement means the skill is working.

The skill is saved as a directory following the Agent Skills specification:.

The important test is: does this skill help local or cheaper models to build kernels?

It has been revealed that A 45% improvement on "unsloth/GLM-4.7-Flash-GGUF:Q4_0" means the skill successfully transfers domain knowledge from a capable model to a faster, cheaper one. Skills that work on weaker models will definitely work on stronger ones.

This is the core value proposition: use expensive models to create skills, then deploy those skills with cheap or local models.

upskill uses a teacher-student approach to evaluate models where the teacher model generates test cases for the student model to be evaluated on.

If you pass an existing skill to upskill eval, it will generate test cases for the skill and evaluate the model on them. Test cases are simple input/output pairs that verify the agent understands the task:.

We can also test how a skill performs across different models:.

This helps you find the cost-performance sweet spot: maybe Haiku with the skill is good enough for your use case, saving significant API costs.

We've shown that upskill can create validated skills that transfer domain expertise from powerful models to cheaper ones. The kernel-builder skill is just one example of what's possible.

The approach works for any specialized task where you'd otherwise write detailed prompts repeatedly. Skills are portable across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other tools that support the Agent Skills specification.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, weekly.
  • "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

"Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

Industry observers note that in this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

Recent findings suggest that the idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below shows a typical AI model routing architecture.

Recent findings suggest that model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Industry observers note that rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-initiative people go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

It has been revealed that intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

In a recent development, two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

Industry observers note that the significant platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google notes Gemini Notebook uses its upcoming Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

It has been revealed that cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

Recent findings suggest that we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

According to recent reports, the test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

According to recent reports, put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

Confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

Sources indicate that the second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

Sources indicate that if Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

According to recent reports, jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

Sources indicate that model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Recent findings suggest that speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

The choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

It has been revealed that the loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

According to recent reports, the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

In a recent development, several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

Sources indicate that an LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

According to recent reports, smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

In a recent development, the ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

According to recent reports, openRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

Sources indicate that openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

According to recent reports, an AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR: Daggr is a new, open-source Python library for building AI workflows that connect Gradio apps, ML models, and custom functions. It automatically generates a visual canvas where you can inspect intermediate outputs, rerun individual steps, and manage state for complex pipelines, all in a few lines of Python code!

If you've built AI applications that combine multiple models or processing steps, you know the pain: chaining API calls, debugging pipelines, and losing track of intermediate results. When something goes wrong in step 5 of a 10-step workflow, you often have to re-run everything just to see what happened.

Most developers either build fragile scripts that are hard to debug or turn to heavy orchestration platforms designed for production pipelines—not rapid experimentation.

We've been working on Daggr to solve problems we kept running into when building AI demos and workflows:.

Recent findings suggest that visualize your code flow: Unlike node-based GUI editors, where you drag and connect nodes visually, Daggr takes a code-first approach. You define workflows in Python, and a visual canvas is generated automatically. This means you get the best of both worlds: version-controllable code and visual inspection of intermediate outputs.

It has been revealed that inspect and Rerun Any Step: The visual canvas isn't just for show. You can inspect the output of any node, modify inputs, and rerun individual steps without executing the entire pipeline. This is invaluable when you're debugging a 10-step workflow and only step 7 is misbehaving. You can even provide “backup nodes” – replacing one model or Space with another – to build resilient workflows.

First-Class Gradio Integration: Since Daggr is built by the Gradio team, it works seamlessly with Gradio Spaces. Point to any public (or private) Space and you can use it as a node in your workflow. No adapters, no wrappers—just reference the Space name and API endpoint.

State Persistence: Daggr automatically saves your workflow state, input values, cached results, canvas position—so you can pick up where you left off. Use "sheets" to maintain multiple workspaces within the same app.

Install daggr with pip or uv, it just requires Python 3.10 or higher:.

After more than a decade of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launched on November 19, 2026, bringing players back to Vice City and the wider fictional state of Leonida.

Rockstar’s latest open-world game is packed with intricate environmental details, hidden references, and Easter eggs, with players continuing to uncover secrets scattered throughout its sprawling map. A developer who worked on the game has shared a tribute to his late mother that players can find.

In a heartfelt Instagram post, GTA 6 developer Matt Green revealed that his late mother has been honoured with a special memorial just north of the in-game region, Hamlet.

Green’s mother, Bev, passed away approximately eight months before the game’s release, meaning she never had the opportunity to see the project her son had been working on.

However, the developer was able to ensure that his mother would remain part of the game through a permanent tribute within its fictional world.

“I’m incredibly grateful that she’s able to be honoured inside the world of VI – at a special memorial just north of Hamlet,” they said. “Miss you Mum.”.

A post shared by Matt Green (@mattxgreen).

The developer recalled begging his mother to buy him a copy of GTA Vice City as a child. Despite her initial reluctance, she eventually agreed, a decision he believes ultimately set him on the path to working at Rockstar Games.

Recent findings suggest that “She was super proud and excited to see what I’d been working on but unfortunately I never got to show her,” they wrote. “She’s been gone almost 8 months now and sometimes it still doesn’t feel real.”.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

Recent findings suggest that …you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your prepares change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.).

According to recent reports, email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”.

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

Recent findings suggest that you can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this new Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when confirmed in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”.

Training Design for Text-to-Image Models: Lessons from Ablations
