AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • Sources indicate that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • It has been revealed that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

Sources indicate that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

It has been revealed that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

It has been revealed that "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

Industry observers note that for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The upcoming findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

Industry observers note that an important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

In a recent development, when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Recent findings suggest that producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

It has been revealed that when the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The newly introduced approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler noted. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

According to recent reports, the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring owners to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler remarked. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

Industry observers note that the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

In a recent development, rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Sources indicate that this guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

In a recent development, • Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid strategy prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Recent findings suggest that originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, notes very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

According to recent reports, turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page claims false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

It has been revealed that the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

Industry observers note that • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

Industry observers note that • Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

It has been revealed that • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

In a recent development, openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and patch as fresh models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

In a recent development, • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

Sources indicate that • Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

It has been revealed that • Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

Recent findings suggest that • Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

Recent findings suggest that they can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

It has been revealed that sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

Sources indicate that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • Recent findings suggest that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising newly introduced method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

Recent findings suggest that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Latest Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

In a recent development, quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can promptly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," indicates Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

According to recent reports, rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

In a recent development, after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, indicated that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an vital step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

According to recent reports, the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

According to recent reports, "This is particularly notable because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Sources indicate that looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

According to recent reports, "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," states Peter Zoller.

This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how swiftly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

While many services are turning to AI in place of an actual human being, Pebblebee’s fresh Alert Dispatch brings the help of a real person into an emergency situation, and it all starts with your Find Hub tracker.

Pebblebee introduced its Alert feature in 2025 as a way to use a Clip 5 tracker for Find Hub as a siren in an emergency. The company later added an optional live location-sharing feature to this, and also released “Halo” as an emergency siren first, tracker second with a special design.

Now, “Alert Dispatch” takes the whole system up a notch.

It has been revealed that instead of relying solely on location sharing and the siren, Pebblebee’s Alert Dispatch assigns an actual human being to the situation, with a trained dispatch agent reaching out first over SMS or a call, then pulling in emergency responders if the situation calls for it. The feature works with Clip 4, Clip 5, and Halo.

Alert Dispatch connects Pebblebee people with a trained dispatch agent when they trigger an Alert, starting with a text and escalating to an Emergency call if they don’t respond. With an attempt to send help when users cannot confirm they’re safe, plus live location sharing and private Check-In calls on Clip 5 and Halo, it adds another layer of support when calling for help isn’t an option.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

In a recent development, the bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Sources indicate that each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

Recent findings suggest that the direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:.

Industry observers note that the obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

Sources indicate that the first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

In a recent development, the second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:.

It has been revealed that on a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a upcoming connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

In a recent development, A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a fresh connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for newly introduced connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:.

Recent findings suggest that second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:.

It has been revealed that we then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

Recent findings suggest that for each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:.

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:.

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:.

It has been revealed that the machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

According to recent reports, if 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

According to recent reports, before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Breaking: Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers

📅 26 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past few years, scaling dense language models has driven most progress in LLMs.
  • More data + more parameters gives better performance.
  • Scaling laws reinforced this trend, but dense scaling has practical limits:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past few years, scaling dense language models has driven most progress in LLMs. From early models like the original ULMFiT (~30M parameters) or GPT-2 (1.5B parameters, which at the time was considered "too dangerous to release" 🧌), and eventually to today’s hundred-billion–parameter systems, the recipe was simple:.

More data + more parameters gives better performance.

Scaling laws reinforced this trend, but dense scaling has practical limits:.

This is where Mixture of Experts (MoEs) enter the picture.

If you're already familiar with MoEs and want to jump straight into the engineering work done in transformers, you can head directly to Transformers and MoEs.

Recent findings suggest that A Mixture of Experts model keeps the Transformer backbone, but replaces certain dense feed-forward layers with a set of experts. An “expert” is not a topic-specialized module (e.g., "math expert", "code expert"). It is simply a learnable sub-network. For each token, a router selects a small subset of experts to process it.

Different tokens activate different experts, based on their hidden representations.

Model capacity depends on total parameters, but inference speed depends on active parameters.

For example, take gpt-oss-20b. It has 21B total parameters, but uses 4 active experts per token, out of a total of 32 experts. Considering the shared components plus the active experts, this model uses ~3.6B active parameters per token. Running this model on an M3 Ultra Mac, which has a memory bandwidth of about 800 GB, we could estimate generation speed as ~ 800 / (3.6 * 2) in bfloat16, where each parameter takes 2 bytes. This yields about 111 tokens per second. The actual performance number we get is ~115 tok/s, which is very close to the back-of-the-envelope calculation.

This super fast speed confirms the model works approximately as a 3.6B parameter one, but it has the same capacity (or quality) as a 21B parameter model.

(Note: speed would be even faster if we used kernels for the native mxfp4 quantization the model uses).

MoEs are attractive for these reasons:.

Given a fixed training FLOP budget, MoEs often outperform dense counterparts.

This means faster iteration and better scaling efficiency.

Experts provide a structural boundary in the computation graph. Since different tokens engage different experts, we can parallelize across experts (we discuss this later in Expert Parallelism).

Recent major MoE releases of open models that happened in the past few weeks include Qwen 3.5, MiniMax M2, GLM-5, or Kimi K2.5.

According to recent reports, the trend accelerated after the success of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025, building on earlier systems like DeepSeek V2. Another early MoE was Mixtral-8x7B, released in December 2023.

It has been revealed that closed labs use MoEs too. ChatGPT has long been rumored to use a sparse architecture, and the open gpt-oss models certainly do.

If you want to learn more about MoEs in general, we strongly suggest reading this blog and watching our recent YouTube video on routing.

In a recent development, most tooling in the ecosystem, including model loading, device placement, quantization, and backend execution was originally designed for dense models. MoEs challenge these assumptions.

Making MoEs first-class citizens in transformers means redesigning parts of the loading pipeline, execution model, and distributed abstractions, not just adding new model classes. We’ll focus on how the transformers library has evolved to support sparse architectures across:.

AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("model_id") downloads and loads model weights into a PyTorch model. For dense models, loading is relatively straightforward where each tensor in the checkpoint maps one-to-one to a parameter in the runtime module.

According to recent reports, for MoEs, it’s more complicated. In most MoE checkpoints, each expert is serialized independently. If you peek inside the DeepSeek-V3 checkpoint index, you’ll see keys like:.

In a recent development, each expert has its own set of weight matrices, essentially 256 (0 to 255 total, taking DeepSeek-V3 as an example) small feed-forward networks saved side by side. At runtime, however, GPUs execute optimized kernels. Modern MoE kernels such as grouped GEMMs and fused MoE implementations are designed to process all experts in a single operation, not by looping over them one at a time.

To do that efficiently, they require expert weights to be packed into a single contiguous tensor.

Bridging this gap systematically is what the weight loading refactor enables.

With the introduction of a generic WeightConverter, the mental model shifted from:.

A checkpoint already matches my runtime layout; loading is mostly a key-by-key copy.

A checkpoint is just a serialized source of tensors. Loading is a conversion pipeline that transforms them into the runtime layout we want.

The central abstraction introduced by this refactor is dynamic weight loading via a WeightConverter.

WeightConverter lets us define:.

It has been revealed that primitive operations (chunk, concatenate, etc.) are composable. Two that are particularly useful for MoEs:.

MergeModulelist merges a list of tensors into a single tensor. For example, you can compose MergeModulelist with Concatenate to stack the experts in a MoE and pack them into one tensor.

In a recent development, splitModulelist splits a tensor back into a list of tensors. For example, you can split a stack of experts back into individual experts.

The refactor improves not just what conversions exist, but how they’re scheduled.

It has been revealed that the loader scans checkpoint keys once, matches them against converter patterns, and groups tensors per converter. Once a key is identified as needed, it’s registered as a future and materialized via a thread pool. Conversion operations run only once their dependencies are ready. For example, MergeModulelist waits until all experts for a layer are loaded.

This avoids repeated scans and reduces memory peaks.

To evaluate the improvements introduced by the new weight-loading pipeline, we benchmarked the v4 vs v5 versions of transformers. The focus is on loading speed of large MoE models, which is often a bottleneck in training and inference.

Two relevant environment variables:.

HF_ENABLE_PARALLEL_LOADING: Enables parallel shard loading via threads.

HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD:Disables the upcoming async pipeline (v5 escape hatch).

Model: Qwen/Qwen1.5-110B-Chat GPU: 1× A100 (80GB).

The speedup is not just “more threads.”.

It’s the combination of Single-pass routing, Async materialization, and Conversion-aware scheduling which together avoid unnecessary materialization and memory peaks while enabling expert packing and projection fusion at load time.

Recent findings suggest that with this refactor we can now create the runtime module structure first and then convert the weights into the structure. We can now optionally attach quantization within the conversion pipeline, making quantization part of the weight loading pipeline itself. This is crucial because quantizing “per expert” only makes sense once experts exist in a predictable packed layout.

This end to end pipeline was not possible earlier and now it comes to the users as an exposed API.

Once experts are packed into a single runtime tensor, another question arises:.

How do you actually route through them efficiently?

It has been revealed that in a Mixture of Experts model, each token is routed to different experts. This means the runtime must dispatch tokens to their selected expert weights, execute the projections efficiently, apply the routing weights and then collect and reorder the results.

This is what the Experts Backend system (introduced in PR #42697) addresses. The Experts Backend introduces a pluggable execution architecture that decouples expert computation from the model implementation. Instead of hardcoding one dispatch strategy inside each MoE model, the system allows expert layers to dynamically select a backend at runtime.

This is implemented via a decorator pattern:.

The decorator wraps expert classes and dispatches computation to the selected backend automatically.

Three backends are presently provided:.

It has been revealed that eager which loops over the selected experts and applies projections per expert. This is used for correctness reference and debugging.

batched_mm uses the torch.bmm API. This duplicate selected expert weights per token and performs a single batched GEMM. This backend is very well suited for small batch, GPU-heavy workloads where memory is available.

Industry observers note that grouped_mm uses torch._grouped_mm API. Here we sort tokens by expert ID, group them, and then perform a single grouped GEMM. This backend shines with large batches or memory-constrained setups.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) models can have hundreds of billions of parameters (far more than what fits on a single GPU). Expert parallelism (EP) addresses this by distributing experts across multiple devices. Each device loads only its assigned subset of experts, computes for those experts and then participates in result aggregation. This approach scales models to far larger parameter counts without increasing computation cost because each token activates only a few experts.

Expert parallelism is enabled via enable_expert_parallel:.

Where N evenly divides the total number of experts, and possibly matches the number of GPUs in your node.

When enable_expert_parallel=True, the model switches from the standard tensor-parallel (TP) plan to an expert-parallel (EP) plan with specialized sharding strategies.

Sources indicate that groupedGemmParallel: This splits the expert weights along the expert dimension (dim=0). Here each device loads only num_experts / num_devices.

RouterParallel: This remaps global expert indices to local indices, masks out experts not assigned to the current rank, ensures each device computes only with its local experts and uses an all-reduce to combine partial outputs across devices.

MoEs are excellent for scaling inference, but training them is significantly more complex.

Recent findings suggest that moEs have a Massive parameter count, the distributed expert communication is complicated, there are routing in-stabilities that need to be handled. To address this, we collaborated with Unsloth to enable significantly faster Mixture-of-Experts training:.

We leverage the Expert Backend abstraction, standardize around PyTorch’s torch._grouped_mm API and use custom Triton grouped-GEMM + LoRA kernels. Unsloth builds on top of the Transformers (and TRL) optimizations to push performance further.

For full details, we recommend reading: Unsloth’s official guide.

Recent findings suggest that as sparse architectures continue to evolve, we want the transformers library to evolve with them. If you’re building with MoEs or experimenting with newly introduced sparse ideas, we’d love to hear from you. Let us know what abstractions, kernels, or workflows you’d like to see next in transformers.

The enable_expert_parallel flag hiding the complexity of GroupedGemmParallel + RouterParallel behind a single config is a great DX win — distributing experts across devices used to require a lot of custom plumbing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a latest Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

Industry observers note that meta launched its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

According to recent reports, meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the firm’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

According to recent reports, so this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

It has been revealed that does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

#80612. Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1751 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • According to recent reports, early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle. When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle. That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question. Define the bar, then pay against it When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a latest AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the tech giant will keep benefiting from that work every year. Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band. Tech Report: PRX Part 3 — Training a Text-to-Image Model in 24h!

📅 03 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models.
  • In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:.
  • What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models. We tried to evaluate each idea in isolation, measuring throughput, convergence speed, and final image quality, and tried to understand what actually moves the needle.

In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:.

What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?

Instead of optimizing one dimension at a time, we’ll stack the most promising ingredients together and see how far we can push performance under a strict compute budget.

To make things concrete, we’re doing a 24-hour speedrun:.

This is very far from the early diffusion days, where training competitive models could cost millions of dollars. The goal here is to demonstrate how much the field has evolved and how far careful engineering can take you in just a single day of training.

Industry observers note that this speedrun is not just a fun experiment. It will likely serve as the foundation for our large-scale training recipe going forward.

Alongside the results, we’re also open-sourcing our code (Github link), which contains:.

So you can reproduce, modify, and extend everything yourself.

Now let’s walk through what went into this 24h run.

In a recent development, we use the x-prediction formulation from Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise [Li and He, 2025]. As seen in Part 2, this enables training directly in pixel space and eliminates the need for a VAE altogether. We use a patch size of 32 and use a 256-dimensional bottleneck in the initial token projection layer. This design keeps the sequence length under control, making pixel-space training computationally manageable even at higher resolutions.

At 512px, the sequence length is:.

(512/32)2=256 (512 / 32)^2 = 256 (512/32)2=256.

At 1024px, the sequence length becomes:.

(1024/32)2=1024 (1024 / 32)^2 = 1024 (1024/32)2=1024.

Instead of following the usual 256px → 512px → 1024px schedule, we start directly at 512px and then fine-tune at 1024px.

According to recent reports, with controlled token counts and modern hardware, pixel-space training is no longer prohibitive. It is simply a cleaner and more direct formulation.

One very nice side effect of predicting x0x_0x0​ directly in pixel space is that we can reuse a whole toolbox from classical computer vision.

Sources indicate that when your model outputs latents, perceptual supervision becomes awkward. You either have to decode back to pixels or define losses in a learned latent space that may or may not align with human perception. Once you predict pixels directly, everything becomes straightforward again. You can plug in perceptual losses exactly as they were originally designed.

It has been revealed that we take inspiration from the paper PixelGen: Pixel Diffusion Beats Latent Diffusion with Perceptual Loss [Ma et al.], where the authors introduce additional perceptual objectives on top of the diffusion loss. They show that adding perceptual signals can noticeably improve convergence speed and final visual quality.

For this 24h run, we add two auxiliary losses:.

The idea is simple: In addition to the standard flow matching objective, we encourage the predicted clean image to match the target image in a perceptual feature space. LPIPS captures low-level perceptual similarity, while DINO features provide a stronger semantic signal.

We keep the same overall idea as the paper, but we tweaked a few details. In our experiments, we empirically found that it worked better to:.

These are small implementation details, but in our setting they consistently gave better results.

We used a weight of 0.1 for the LPIPS loss and 0.01 for the DINO perceptual loss, matching the values recommended in the original paper.

These losses are lightweight compared to the main transformer forward pass, and in our setup they add only a small overhead while providing a consistent quality boost.

To make each step cheaper, we use token routing with TREAD [Krause et al., 2025]), which randomly selects a fraction of tokens and lets them bypass a contiguous chunk of transformer blocks, then re-injects them later so nothing is dropped.

In a recent development, we picked TREAD over SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) mostly for simplicity, and because the extra complexity of SPRINT did not feel worth the fairly small additional compute savings in our setting (sequence length 64 vs. 128 with TREAD at 512px).

Following the TREAD recipe, we route 50% of the tokens from the 2nd block to the penultimate block of the transformer.

Routed models can look worse under vanilla CFG, especially when undertrained, so we implemented a simple self-guidance scheme inspired by Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025), which guides using a dense vs. routed conditional prediction instead of relying on an unconditional branch.

We used REPA [Yu et al., 2024] for representation alignment.

Recent findings suggest that for the teacher, we went with DINOv3 [Siméoni et al. 2025] since it gave the best quality improvements in our previous experiments.

Concretely, we apply the alignment loss once,at the 8th transformer block with a loss weight of 0.5.

According to recent reports, since we combine REPA with TREAD routing, we only compute the alignment loss on the non-routed tokens, meaning the tokens that actually go through the blocks where we apply the loss. This keeps the REPA signal consistent and avoids comparing features for tokens that skipped the computation path.

We used the Muon optimizer, using the FSDP implementation from muon_fsdp_2, since it showed a clear improvement over Adam in our previous runs.

Muon is only applied to 2D parameters (basically matrices). Everything else (biases, norms, embeddings, etc.) is optimized with Adam, which is why the config has two parameter groups.

We trained on three publicly available synthetic datasets:.

The schedule is basically: go fast at 512, then sharpen at 1024:.

We also keep an EMA of the weights for sampling and eval:.

Below are the evaluation curves we tracked throughout the run and a few sample grids from the final checkpoint:.

For a one day training run, this is already a pretty solid place to be. The model is not flawless yet (you can still spot some texture glitches, occasional weird anatomy, and it can get a bit shaky on very hard prompts), but it is clearly usable. Prompt following is strong, the overall aesthetic is consistent, and the 1024 stage mostly does what we want: sharpen details without breaking composition.

According to recent reports, the key takeaway is that we're very close. The remaining complications look more like undertraining artifacts and limited data diversity than signs of a structural flaw in the recipe. The failure modes are consistent with what you’d expect from a model that simply hasn’t seen enough varied data yet. With more compute and broader coverage, this exact setup should continue improving in a fairly predictable way.

Sources indicate that zooming out, this speed run also highlights how far diffusion training has come. By combining pixel-space training, efficient routing, representation alignment, and lightweight perceptual guidance, you can now get a meaningful model in about a day on a budget that would have sounded unrealistic not that long ago.

This 24h run is just a starting point, not the finish line. Next, we will keep pushing the same recipe with a bit more scale and iterate on the dataset mix and captioning.

All the code and configs behind this speedrun, as well as the full experimental framework used throughout Part 1 and Part 2, are available in the PRX repository: https://github.com/Photoroom/PRX.

While we don’t redistribute the exact training datasets used in this run, the pipeline is fully configurable and designed to be easily adapted to your own data. You can plug in different datasets, tweak individual components (TREAD, REPA, perceptual losses, Muon, etc.), and run controlled experiments with minimal friction. Our goal is to make this a practical playground for fast diffusion research, and we hope the community will use it to explore, benchmark, and iterate on these techniques in their own setups.

Sources indicate that if you made it this far, thank you for reading. We would also love to have you join our Discord community, where we share PRX progress and results, and discuss anything diffusion and text-to-image related.

It has been revealed that goodbye for now, and stay tuned for the next round of experiments! 🚀.

In a recent development, this speedrun was inspired by several recent efforts exploring fast and low-cost training of diffusion models. If you're interested in speedrunning text-to-image models, we encourage you to check out the following works:.

In a recent development, 24 hours is very impressive, but looking at 32 H200 makes it make a bit more sense xD. Super cool that you used Muon! And, are you planning on releasing the re-captioned brivangl/midjourney-v6-llava?

Yeah, definitely not possible on consumer hardware… yet :D That’s also why we added the $1500 tag.

In a recent development, regarding releasing the captions, we hadn’t really thought about that. If you think it would be valuable for the community, we can work on releasing them as well.

Hi, this article is very inspiring.I'd like to get your thoughts on the perceptual loss. During a research internship on (raw) image restoration - and trying to explore the perception/distortion tradeoff , I did a few attempts at VGG and Dino loss aswell. I always ended up with checkerboard patterns (no matter vgg or dino). If you look at the original paper from Johnson , it's full of these artifacts.Did you face any such issue or can share useful insights about that topic ?

It has been revealed that I don’t think we really observed such artifacts, or at least not due to LPIPS. We did see something similar without LPIPS when using JIT on undertrained models, but I don’t think we observe them anymore. It might simply be because the model had not converged yet.One situation where we started to observe checkerboard patterns was during reward alignment with GRPO or SRPO on one of these models. In that case the artifacts were much more noticeable, but I don’t think they were related to LPIPS since we were not using it at the time.What type of model were you using?

There’s zero reason to store your SS card like this. Unnecessary exposure.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted explicit references to “Social Security Number” in Google Play Services v26.46.30 in connection with Google Wallet.

According to recent reports, while exact functionality is unclear at this time, this appears to include support for seeing your Social Security benefits, or at least logging those benefits, in a digital form. There are mentions of Retirement, Survivors, and/or Disability Insurance (RSDI), Supplemental Security Income, Medicare, and more, as well as qualifiers for deductions and effective dates.

#80609. The weakest link in cybersecurity is still a human one

The weakest link in cybersecurity is still a human one

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony.
  • In a recent development, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony.
  • Industry observers note that huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he cofounded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a organization whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature. Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he cofounded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company states no secrets were leaked. In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.” Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information. These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment? Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch, or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting—and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information, or take risks. The comfort of a human voice Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets. He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the fresh IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him. In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice. Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat, and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email. Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many yes responses over the phone as they did by email. When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have. The Midas touch Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence, and risk-taking. In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change. The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets. Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder. The power of face-to-face Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about. In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far. Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face. In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call. Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against. Vanessa Bohns is a Braunstein Family Professor and chair of organizational behavior at Cornell University. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround proposal aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The owner of a dwindling empire of Wendy’s restaurants on Friday disclosed its plans to close several more stores, bringing its total number of shuttered locations to almost 100. It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround proposal aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image. The franchisee behind the closures, Meritage Hospitality Group of Grand Rapids, Michigan, is among the largest operators within the Wendy’s system, at one time owning roughly 375 locations across 15 states. It closed dozens of those restaurants in the months before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in September, and has since shuttered additional waves of stores at regular intervals as part of cash collateral agreements with its lenders. How many Wendy’s stores has Meritage closed? According to court documents, Meritage has closed well over 90 Wendy’s locations since late last year, with many of those stores shuttered before its September bankruptcy petition. As is typical in Chapter 11 cases, Meritage is seeking to reject the leases on many of the stores that it closed pre-bankruptcy—roughly 60, court filings show—a list that includes a handful of Taco John’s and Morning Belle locations, in addition to Wendy’s. Since the bankruptcy, Meritage has also closed at least 41 additional Wendy’s restaurants, including six closures that were disclosed on Friday. The newly shuttered restaurants were located in Florida, Georgia, Michigan, and Ohio: 12135 Lem Turner Road Jacksonville, FL 32218 1928 Hwy 155 McDonough, GA 30252 3675 Cascade Road Atlanta, GA 30331 9556 US 31 So Interlochen, MI 49643 8258 Broadmoor Avenue Caledonia, MI 49316 914 Conant St. Maumee, OH 43537 Prior to the above six restaurants, Meritage disclosed waves of store closures on at least five separate occasions: 5 locations on September 25 5 locations on October 2 10 locations on October 9 13 stores on October 16 2 stores on October 30 Fast Company has reached out to Meritage Hospitality Group and Wendy’s for comment. What will happen to Meritage’s remaining stores? Meritage has owned Wendy’s restaurants since the late 1990s, but its relationship with the fast food giant appeared to turn increasingly contentious in recent years as its business faced headwinds on numerous fronts, including the soaring cost of beef. The franchisee has blamed Wendy’s for a strategy of “deep discounting” that it states squeezed profits. The Wendy’s Company, for its part, had sought to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements, claiming to be owed more than $146 million in past-due royalties and other fees. Despite all this animosity, the two sides are working together to salvage what’s left of the Meritage fleet. Wendy’s disclosed earlier this month that it wants to buy up to 163 restaurants from Meritage. That deal, which is still subject to better bids, is expected to close early next year. Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations. It’s unclear if additional Wendy’s locations could close before or after these asset sales are complete. This story is developing….

Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations.
